case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC Application 218/92, decided on 17 February 1993

clause.text: Any person detained shall be brought before a judge and cannot be held without legal order.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner's detention was lawful under Article 13(2), specifically if he was detained with proper legal authority and brought before a judge.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed his detention was unlawful as it followed an unlawful arrest and that he was not shown the detention orders.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the petitioner was detained under valid detention orders issued under the Emergency Regulations and that he was aware of these orders. The petitioner was also produced before a Magistrate who ordered further detention.
key_facts: Petitioner was detained on the 6th floor of Police Headquarters under orders issued under Regulation 19(2) of the Emergency Regulations.
Detention orders 1R2, 1R3, and 1R4 were issued for 90 days starting 10.01.92.
Petitioner was produced before a Magistrate on 03.02.92 and ordered detained for 30 more days.
Petitioner was shown to family and academic staff on 04.02.92.
Petitioner was aware of the detention orders despite claiming he was not shown them.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court interpreted Article 13(2) as requiring detention to be authorized by legal order and for detainees to be brought before a judge. The Court found that the detention orders under the Emergency Regulations were valid legal authority and that the petitioner was produced before a Magistrate as required.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found the detention orders valid and that the petitioner was aware of them. The petitioner was produced before a Magistrate who extended detention. The claim that the petitioner was not shown the orders was denied by the respondents and contradicted by the petitioner's own affidavit.
principles_established: Detention must be authorized by a valid legal order.
Detainees must be brought before a judicial authority within a reasonable time.
Awareness of detention orders by the detainee is relevant to compliance.

outcome.holding: The Court held that the petitioner's detention was lawful under Article 13(2) and that there was no infringement of this constitutional right.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(2) was directly engaged to assess the legality of the petitioner's detention and whether it complied with constitutional safeguards requiring judicial oversight and legal authority.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner was detained under valid detention orders issued under Emergency Regulations and was produced before a Magistrate who ordered further detention, satisfying the requirements of Article 13(2).
